summary:
We developed a planetary exploration and analog-matching platform that pairs real-world Earth terrain profiles with extraterrestrial landing sites on the Moon and Mars. The system integrates a versioned site catalog, geospatial terrain extraction pipelines, a physics-based spacecraft lander simulation, and an interactive web viewer backed by Supabase edge functions.

Testing autonomous spacecraft landing systems and evaluating planetary surface hazards is expensive and limited by sparse high-resolution extraterrestrial data. Our platform addresses this challenge by algorithmically matching planetary targets—such as Jezero Crater, Mons Mouton, and Tranquillity Base—to geologically and topographically similar Earth analogs (e.g., Amboy Crater, Kilbourne Hole, and White Sands). By validating terrain fidelity, soil properties, and hazard profiles against accessible Earth sites, engineers and researchers can run realistic entry, descent, and landing (EDL) simulations before deploying hardware. This bridges the gap between terrestrial field testing and off-world mission planning, reducing mission risk and improving landing safety for future lunar and Martian exploration.
details:
What Does It Do & How Does It Work?Analog Atlas is an interactive 3D planetary analog matcher and synchronized twin-flight physics simulator designed for Moon and Mars surface missions. Instead of locking mission planners into a handful of pre-selected landing zones, users can choose from 49 curated exploration targets (such as Shackleton Crater's northern rim) or drop a pin anywhere on the Moon or Mars, including uncharted terrain humans have never visited.

  1. Dynamic Multi-Dataset Analog Matching: When a user selects a region or drops a live pin, our engine queries NASA orbital elevation mosaics (LOLA for the Moon, MOLA for Mars) on demand. To prevent resolution distortion, it averages 30 m Earth Copernicus GLO-30 terrain to match the exact 150 m lunar or 500 m Martian spatial resolution over a 4 km window, then dynamically scores and ranks 102 global Earth analog sites using a non-hardcoded composite of geology/landform type (50%) and topographic metrics—slope distribution, roughness, relief, and bowl/ridge share (50%).
  2. 1:1 3D Hologram Terrain Overlay: The app drapes the target lunar or Martian elevation grid as a cyan wireframe at a true 1:1 vertical scale directly over the Earth analog's digital elevation model, flagging slopes steeper than 12° in red. This visually answers both halves of NASA's challenge: what terrain features match, and exactly where the Earth analogy breaks.
  3. Hardware-Coupled Twin-Flight Simulation: In the Equipment Bay, users configure real lander hardware—such as landing gear stroke, damping ratio, and Lidar hazard-detection range—which feeds directly into a deterministic 120 Hz (1/120 s) physics engine. During Twin Flight, the exact same lander flies simultaneously over the Earth analog and the Moon/Mars target, holding spacecraft physics constant while testing real terrain grids and local interference (such as dust and solar glare).
  4. Field Test Debrief & JSON Telemetry Export: After touchdown, the engine generates a comparative debrief report evaluating sink rate, fuel consumption, touchdown slope, and 25-seed Monte Carlo blind-landing statistics, outputting actionable field-test adjustments and a downloadable JSON telemetry file for upcoming test runs.

Benefits

  • Eliminates Earth-Site Guesswork: Replaces manual, hardcoded comparisons of a few famous deserts with an objective, scale-matched ranking across 102 global Earth sites.
  • Quantifies Analog Limits Early: Exposes slope, structural, and environmental mismatches between Earth test sites and extraterrestrial targets before physical field campaigns begin.
  • Cost-Efficient Monte Carlo Validation: Allows engineers to run thousands of simulated sensor, gear, and hazard-avoidance descents on real terrain data before risking billion-dollar test prototypes and flight landers.
  • Workflow Integration: Exports structured JSON telemetry that engineering teams can feed directly into subsequent hardware simulations and field-test plans.

Intended Impact Analog Atlas turns static planetary elevation maps into an operational mission-rehearsal tool for Artemis, Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS), and future Mars surface missions. By opening site analysis to arbitrary coordinates rather than fixed preset locations, our platform helps mission planners adapt to evolving planetary surfaces and landing targets while uncovering overlooked, higher-fidelity Earth analogs around the world (such as Kilbourne Hole in New Mexico, the Tabernas badlands in Spain, and the Lut Desert in Iran).

Tools, Coding Languages, Hardware & Software Used

  • Frontend & 3D Visualization: TypeScript, React, Three.js / WebGL (interactive 3D Moon and Mars globes, 1:1 vertical-scale terrain hologram overlay, and live 3D descent rendering).
  • Physics Engine & Backend: Custom 120 Hz deterministic rigid-body and landing-gear simulation engine (TypeScript), Python (analog_score.py and automated accuracy/validity test suites), and Supabase Edge Functions (match-analog serverless API for on-demand pin queries).
  • NASA & Open Space/Earth Datasets: NASA LOLA (Lunar Orbiter Laser Altimeter), NASA MOLA (Mars Orbiter Laser Altimeter), NASA Diviner (lunar thermal and rock abundance), NASA POWER (solar and climate data), Copernicus GLO-30 (30 m Earth DEM), ESA WorldCover, and USGS geologic maps.

How Is Our Project Creative? Rather than building a static geography presentation around two or three well-known analog sites, Analog Atlas merges live arbitrary planetary pin-dropping, scale-matched geomorphology scoring, a 1:1 3D hologram overlay, and synchronized twin-world physics simulation into a single interactive rehearsal pipeline. Crucially, instead of treating differences between Earth and the Moon or Mars as a flaw, our system treats "where the analogy breaks" as a primary engineering output—even recommending how to adjust Earth landing coordinates (such as moving a test flag onto 5–10° crater walls) to better replicate lunar rim dynamics.

Factors Our Team Considered

  • Spatial Resolution & Scale Parity: Comparing a 30 m Earth elevation map directly to a 150 m lunar or 500 m Martian grid artificially inflates Earth slope values; we enforced scale-matched spatial averaging over uniform 4 km windows so topographic comparisons remain scientifically valid.
  • Historical Validation: To verify that our scoring and landing-similarity models reflect real-world flight behavior, we validated our pipeline against historical landing data from Apollo 11, Apollo 12, and Apollo 14.
  • Hardware vs. Environmental Variables: We separated controllable spacecraft parameters (gear stroke, damping, tip-over thresholds, Lidar scan and diversion limits) from site-specific environmental factors (slope hazards, dust, glare), while explicitly documenting unreplicable planetary conditions such as reduced gravity, vacuum, and regolith mechanics.
